title: Target groups
text:
Who is targeted?
The interventions were created for citizens at various life stages and levels of ability, such as children, youth, elderly and those with low levels of (digital) literacy, and for citizens in their various roles in society, such as parents, teachers, employees, civil servants and entrepreneurs.
Most interventions, 33% (50 interventions), target children and youth, and another 28% (42) target the general population. They are followed by entrepreneurs and small to medium-sized business owners (11%), the elderly (5%) and those with low (digital) literacy (5%). Parents and teachers are underrepresented as the primary target group, but they are the most prominent secondary target group (17% and 22% of interventions with a secondary target group), especially for interventions that primarily target children or youth.

 Primary target group Secondary target group

title: Target groups
text:
Inclusiveness
28% of the interventions made an explicit effort to include at least one marginalised group. This mostly happened through (1) age-specific support, (2) language and skills accessibility, such as plain language and multilingual materials, (3) financial and practical accessibility, such as free offers or help with acquiring devices, and (4) tailored approaches for specific vulnerable groups.
Inclusiveness is mainly realised through age, language, digital skills and affordability. Structural forms of inclusion, such as co-developing interventions with marginalised groups, are less common.

title: Problems
text:
Which problems are addressed?
The majority of interventions address the problem of cybercrime (36%): reducing the risk of fraud, scams or impersonation, promoting protective measures against cyberattacks targeting SMEs, or resilience trainings for vulnerable groups such as seniors. Many of these interventions are initiated by the Centre for Crime Prevention and Safety (CCV) or the police.
The second most important problem concerns the safety and wellbeing of youth (21%), such as cyberbullying, online hate, violations of online sexual boundaries, social media addiction and problematic phone use. These are followed by AI and digital transformation (14%), digital inclusion (10%), digital literacy (10%) and misinformation, news and media literacy (6.4%).

In addition, we coded which policy questions from the Digital Society policy framework each intervention addresses (up to three per intervention).

title: Problems
section: What do interventions aim to achieve?
text:
What do interventions aim to achieve?
Overall, the interventions largely expect to make citizens more digitally skilled and secure, which closely corresponds to the problems they seek to address. 34% expect improved online security via reduced vulnerability to cybercrime, fraud and phishing; 30% aim to promote digital literacy (basic skills, media literacy, AI literacy); and 21% specifically target the digital safety and health of youth. Fewer interventions focus on access to digital devices and services (8%), responsible digitalisation within organisations (4%) and broader social risks such as public disorder or road safety (2%). For 1%, no concrete outcome is stated.

 Expected outcomes Outcome categories










Source: final report ‘Grip op Digitaal Burgerschap’ (inductive coding of the problem, outcome and runtime descriptions).

title: Recommendations
text:
The landscape of digital citizenship interventions in the Kingdom of the Netherlands is broad and diverse. At the same time, the interventions reveal clear priorities: they focus primarily on avoiding harm and building knowledge about digital risks, with comparatively less attention to democratic participation, skills and behaviour. The digital citizen is largely portrayed as a responsible and resilient user, whereas a broader understanding of digital citizenship would also emphasise active participation and empowerment.

title: Recommendations
text:
Digital justice
Many interventions prioritise some of the most vulnerable groups: children and youth, the elderly and those with low literacy. In addition, 10% of interventions explicitly address the digital divide and digital access. In a country where 99% of households have an internet connection, such interventions target a relatively small group, but they are highly needed for those who would otherwise be excluded.

title: Competencies
text:
Knowledge, skills and behaviour
Because digital citizenship comprises knowledge, skills and behaviour, we coded to what extent interventions targeted these three competencies. 95% targeted knowledge, 58% targeted skills and only 16% directly targeted behaviour.
An intervention was coded as targeting behaviour only if behavioural change was directly implemented as part of the intervention. Interventions that merely informed about behaviour were coded as indirect; this was the case for 66% of the interventions. In the chart, Yes for behaviour therefore means directly targeting behavioural change.

title: Competencies
text:
Active and responsible participation
Active participation was stimulated when citizens learn to meaningfully engage in key life domains such as work or digital government via digital media, tools or technologies. This was encouraged by about half of the interventions (50%).
Responsible participation refers to an ethical use of digital media that reduces harm to oneself or others, for example by informing citizens about false information, online etiquette or protection against cybercrime. This was encouraged by the majority of interventions (81%).

title: Initiators
text:
Initiators, scope and runtime
The public sector is best represented: 60% of interventions come from government agencies, municipalities, schools, libraries and similar institutions. 25% emerged from a public-private collaboration, such as internet safety programmes by ministries and internet providers. Private sector actors, such as health care providers, commercial training centres or tech companies, initiate 15% of the interventions.
The majority of interventions is intended for the national level (46%), often combined with local implementation. Regional (27%) and online interventions (24%) are common as well.
Only 9% of interventions specified an explicit start and end date. Most interventions (58%) did not specify a runtime, even though information and materials remain available online; 31% are recurring or ongoing interventions, and 1% explicitly state that the intervention has been discontinued.

title: Welcome to the Digital Citizenship Dashboard
text:
Welcome to the Digital Citizenship Dashboard, presenting an overview of 151 interventions that help citizens in the Kingdom of the Netherlands participate actively and responsibly in the digital society.
This dashboard presents the results of WP2: Inventory of Digital Citizenship Interventions. We mapped whom these interventions target, which problems they address, what form they take, and to what extent they foster knowledge, skills and behaviour.
We define digital citizenship as a learned set of competencies (skills, knowledge and behaviours) that enable citizens to participate actively and responsibly in the digital society.

title: About
text:
Aim of the study
The aims of WP2 were to (1) provide an overview of current interventions regarding digital citizenship in the Kingdom of the Netherlands, (2) clarify how these interventions relate to expert perspectives in WP1, and (3) identify unused potential in strengthening digital citizenship.


Selecting interventions
Interventions had to focus on citizens and target digital competencies or basic prerequisites for participation in the digital society, and be implemented in (or clearly target citizens of) the Kingdom of the Netherlands. We scouted government websites (www.digitaleoverheid.nl), the Ministry of the Interior and Kingdom Relations, websites of relevant organisations and networks (e.g., Netwerk Mediawijsheid), and consulted experts on digital citizenship.
This search led to an initial sample of 177 interventions. Interventions were excluded if they were located outside the Netherlands, if their website was inaccessible, or if they were not about digital participation, targeted organisations without an immediate focus on individuals, or were a network, research project, database, infrastructure or subsidy. (Nearly) identical interventions rolled out under different names in several municipalities, such as walk-in help sessions in community centres or libraries, were merged.


Coding
The final sample of 151 interventions was analysed by three trained coders following a deductive-inductive approach. The codebook was based on the definition of digital citizenship (knowledge, skills, behaviours, active and responsible participation), descriptive information (type of intervention, initiator, runtime) and policy-relevant information (social problem, inclusiveness, expected outcome), defined after discussion with the Ministry of the Interior. After testing on a subsample, the codebook was refined and expanded. Target groups were coded based on who was explicitly named as the target group; interventions without an explicit target group were coded as aimed at the general population.


About the figures
The charts in this dashboard are computed directly from the coding sheet. Percentages are based on the coded interventions. In the target group coding, children and youth were merged into one category, and all citizens and unspecified into general population. The categories for problems addressed, expected outcomes (inductive) and runtime are taken from the final report Grip op Digitaal Burgerschap.


Research team
Marina Tulin, Olga Eisele, Alain Starke, Ernesto de León, Christian Burgers and Jessica Piotrowski, Amsterdam School of Communication Research (ASCoR), University of Amsterdam.

title: Formats
text:
Form of the interventions
The most common form was online resources (26%), such as information on a website, tips or educational videos. Campaigns targeting understanding or awareness were also common (19%). Offline trainings (15%) and online trainings (11%) differ from these because they are pedagogical programmes that train concrete knowledge, skills or behaviours via consecutive modules.
Notably, 17 interventions were serious games (11%), such as a cybersecurity game in which employees of a fictional SME respond to a ransomware attack via interactive videos.

 Primary type Secondary type

title: Formats
text:
Life domains and digital contexts
Most interventions address general everyday digital use (26% of all mentions), followed by security (15%), critical thinking (12%), social media or social relationships (11%) and education (10%). Surprisingly, work (7%), health (5%) and news media (2%) are poorly represented.
Everyday use means, for example, emailing, creating a social media account, changing a password or learning to use online video calling.
